Viviparous is an adjective that describes a living organism — most commonly an animal — that produces offspring which develop and grow inside the parent's body and are then born alive, rather than being laid as an egg that hatches outside the body.

The simplest, most relatable example: a human baby. It spends roughly nine months developing inside its mother's womb, nourished directly by her body through the placenta, and is then born as a living infant. Humans are viviparous. Every other placental mammal — dogs, cats, horses, whales, dolphins, elephants, lions — is viviparous too.
The Detail That Makes the Definition Precise

Being born alive isn't quite enough on its own to make something "viviparous." The more precise requirement is this: the developing offspring must receive nourishment directly from the parent's body — usually through a placenta or a similar organ — while growing inside the parent.

This distinction matters because it separates truly viviparous animals from a related but different group called ovoviviparous animals (explained below).

Oviparous is the direct opposite of viviparous. Oviparous animals lay eggs. The embryo develops inside the egg — outside the mother's body — and hatches when it is ready. Birds, most reptiles, most fish, and all insects are oviparous. A hen lays an egg; a chick hatches from it. That is oviparity.

Viviparous animals never lay eggs. The young develop inside, are fed by the mother's body, and emerge alive.

Ovoviviparous is the interesting middle ground. Some animals carry their eggs inside their bodies, so the young do hatch internally and emerge live — which looks like viviparity from the outside. But here's the key difference: the embryos are fed by the egg yolk, not by the mother's body directly. The mother is essentially just a vessel; she doesn't nourish the young herself. Certain species of sharks, some snakes, and some lizards fall into this category.

So to summarize the three:

In oviparous animals, eggs are laid outside the body and hatch there. In ovoviviparous animals, eggs stay inside the body, the young hatch inside, but nourishment comes from the yolk. In viviparous animals, there is no egg-hatching at all — the young develop continuously inside the parent, fed directly by the parent's body, and are born alive.

Placental mammals are the clearest and most numerous example of viviparous animals. This group includes humans, all domestic pets, farm animals, great apes, wolves, bears, bats, elephants, and even ocean-dwelling mammals like whales and dolphins. In all these animals, the embryo implants in the mother's uterus, connects to her bloodstream through a placenta, and is sustained by her until birth.

Marsupials — such as kangaroos, wallabies, and koalas — are also viviparous, though with a twist. Their young are born at a very early, underdeveloped stage and then continue growing in the mother's pouch, where they nurse on milk. They are still considered viviparous because birth is live, not from an egg.

Beyond mammals, viviparity also occurs in some fish — guppies, for example, are viviparous freshwater fish that give birth to live young. Certain sharks like the bull shark and the hammerhead shark are also truly viviparous, nourishing their pups through a placenta-like structure. Some lizards and snakes, such as the blue-tongued skink and the common European adder, are viviparous as well.

The word has a distinct but related meaning in botany. A plant is described as viviparous when its seeds begin to germinate — sprout and grow — while still attached to the parent plant, before they have even fallen to the ground.

The most famous example is the mangrove tree. Mangrove seeds sprout right on the parent tree, developing into small seedling structures that dangle from the branches. When they are ready, they drop into the muddy, waterlogged coastal soil below and take root almost immediately. This is a brilliant adaptation: if the seeds had to lie dormant in saltwater or shifting mud, many would die. By sprouting early on the parent, they arrive ready to anchor themselves and survive.

Some grasses and certain bulb plants like wild garlic also show viviparity by producing tiny plantlets or offshoots on the parent plant rather than conventional seeds.

"Unlike most fish, which are oviparous and lay thousands of eggs, some sharks are viviparous, nourishing their pups through a placenta and giving birth to live young."

"All humans are viviparous — babies develop inside the womb and are born alive."

"The mangrove is a viviparous tree; its seeds germinate before they even leave the parent plant."

"Scientists studying viviparity in reptiles have found that it tends to evolve in colder climates, where keeping embryos warm inside the body is an advantage."

Viviparity is the noun form — it refers to the trait, condition, or biological strategy of being viviparous. ("The viviparity of placental mammals is one of their most defining characteristics.")

Viviparously is the rarely used adverb form. ("The species reproduces viviparously.")

Viviparousness is another, less common noun form meaning the same as viviparity.

If an organism develops inside the parent's body, is nourished directly by the parent, and is born alive rather than hatched from an external egg — that organism, and the species it belongs to, is viviparous.
